lessons.title: Der Kopf — “the head”
lessons.gloss: the head — masculine, capitalised, with final pf

segments.text: Learn the first body part with its article and its characteristic final sound.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: der Kopf

segments.text: der Kopf — the head.
It is masculine and capitalised because every German noun begins with a capital letter.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: Make the -pf sequence

segments.text: At the end of Kopf, close for p and release directly into f. English has no identical native ending, so practise it slowly:
Ko-p-f becomes Kopf.
A useful phrase is:
Ich habe Kopfschmerzen. — I have a headache.
German compounds simply place nouns together: Kopf (head) + Schmerzen (pains).

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: The old cup

segments.text: Kopf originally meant a cup or bowl. It is related to English cup; both were early borrowings of Late Latin cuppa. A container word became slang for the skull and eventually took over the everyday job.
German’s older inherited head-word did not disappear completely. The next micro-lesson follows it into compounds and compares the same container metaphor in French.
“Der Kopf — masculine, capitalised.”

Say “the head.” (Der Kopf.) Give its gender. (Masculine.) Why the capital? (It is a noun.) What did Kopf first mean? (A cup or bowl.) Name the related English word. (Cup.) Next: find the inherited word Haupt.

lessons.title: Kopf / Haupt — two head-words
lessons.gloss: the cup-word and the inherited Germanic head-word

segments.text: Kopf began as “cup.” German’s inherited word for “head” is Haupt, a cousin of English head and Latin caput.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: inherited Haupt

segments.text: The initial k becomes h relationship reflects Grimm’s law, the same systematic Germanic sound shift seen in Latin pater beside English father. The later consonants have their own history; use the initial pair as the clear signal.
Haupt survives in compounds and formal vocabulary:
Hauptstadt — capital, literally “head city”;
Hauptbahnhof — main station;
Hauptsache — main thing.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way: Two container metaphors

utterances: language: German. everyday word: Kopf. older picture: cuppa, cup.
language: French. everyday word: tête. older picture: testa, pot.

segments.text: Both languages independently promoted a vessel-word to “head,” while keeping the older head-root in words for chiefs, capitals, or main things. The vocabulary sources are both Latin loans, but the metaphor was applied separately: heads look like bowls in many languages.
“Kopf took the job; Haupt stayed in compounds.”

Which word is everyday “head”? (Kopf.) Which inherited word survives in compounds? (Haupt.) Name two compounds. (Hauptstadt, Hauptbahnhof.) What parallel metaphor did French use? (Tête, originally a pot.) Next: the hand.

segments.prompt: Which inherited German head-word survives in compounds such as Hauptstadt?

feedback.correct: Correct: Haupt is the inherited head-word retained in compounds.
feedback.incorrect: The inherited word is Haupt, as in Hauptstadt and Hauptbahnhof.

lessons.title: die Hand — "the hand"
lessons.gloss: the hand — the same word as English, and unrelated to Romance manus

segments.text: After the tangle of Kopf and Haupt, here is the easiest word in the chapter — and a useful lesson about when languages don't match.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: die Hand

segments.text: die Hand — the hand. Feminine, and spelled exactly like English.

One pronunciation note: the final d is said as a t. German devoices a consonant at the end of a word, so Hand ends like English hunt — but with the open ah of Tag, not hunt's vowel. Add an ending and the d comes back: die Hände ("the hands").

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: It is the English word

segments.text: Hand is Germanic handuz, and English inherited it directly. Same word, same meaning, two thousand years apart. German and English are close relatives, and body parts are where you feel it most:

blocks.title: Why it's said this way: Where the family tree stops

segments.text: Now the interesting part. Every Romance language builds "hand" on Latin manus:
And Germanic — German, English — has handuz, which is not related to manus at all. The two families simply have different words here.

That is worth noticing, because these connections keep turning up, and it can start to feel as though everything must connect. It doesn't. Indo-European languages share a great deal, and then diverge, and "hand" is one of the places where they diverged early and completely.
The Latin word did reach German — but only as borrowed vocabulary: Manuskript, Maniküre, manuell. Learned imports, sitting beside the native word without displacing it.

segments.instruction: "die Hand" — final d said as t
the plural, and hear the d return — "die Hände"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the plural, and hear the *d* return — "die Hän**d**e"]

segments.instruction: the gap — "main, mano, mão … but Hand"

segments.text: Say "the hand." (Die Hand — feminine.) How is the final d pronounced, and why? (As a t — German devoices final consonants; the d returns in Hände.) Is Hand related to French main? (No — Germanic handuz against Latin manus; the families differ here.) How did manus reach German anyway? (As borrowed learned words — Manuskript, manuell.) Next: the rest of the body.
